question: Is medicinal cannabis oil permissible for a cancer patient, and must prayers missed while sedated be made up?
asked: Someone in his family has terminal cancer, and the doctors have advised him to use cannabis oil that has both THC and CBD. Part one: is it halal to use cannabis oil as a medicine, especially for the treatment of cancer? Part two: if it is halal, one of the side effects of THC is that it puts you to sleep for extended periods of time. What can one do with regard to salah? Is the salah forgiven, or must it be prayed?
answer:
So this question is about cannabis — cannabis is the technical term; of course, the popular term is marijuana. And of course, cannabis is a psychoactive drug that is made from the cannabis plant, and the main psychoactive ingredient is THC, or tetrahydrocannabinol. THC, tetrahydrocannabinol: so remember this, THC.

Now, there is absolutely no difference of opinion amongst medical experts, amongst scientists, that THC has mental effects. It affects the brain. And these effects include euphoria, altered states of mind, distortion of the sense of time, diluting one's sense of concentration, impaired memory, impaired body movement. It also gives you a sense of relaxation. And so it doesn't just affect your mental state; it also affects your physical state, because it impairs your reaction time and it makes you lethargic.

And therefore it is very clear, there is no doubt, that cannabis is a narcotic. This is something that is crystal clear: cannabis is a narcotic, marijuana is a narcotic. And the term for narcotics in the Shari'ah is mukhaddirat. So a mukhaddir is a drug that induces symptoms like numbness, like drowsiness, like stupor, like lethargy, like basically wanting to fall asleep. This is a mukhaddir.

Now, there is a technical difference between the muskirat and the mukhaddirat. This is a bit of fiqh here, and inshallah it'll come in handy. We all know that alcohol is a muskir. By alcohol, of course, I mean alcoholic drinks. We talked about it in another Q&A; I talked about alcohol that is used as a solvent. We're now talking about beer and whiskey and wine. We're talking about fermented drinks, khamr. Khamr is a muskir. And our Prophet ﷺ said, whatever intoxicates in large quantities is haram in small quantities. This is muskir.

Now, according to the stronger position amongst the scholars of our religion, the mukhaddirat and the muskirat are not exactly the same in ruling. Not every mukhaddir is going to be considered of the muskirat. Therefore, the mukhaddirat are broader than the muskirat, and the mukhaddirat have a different status than the muskirat. The Shari'ah looks at the mukhaddirat in a different category, with a different lens, than it does the muskirat. And when it comes to the mukhaddirat, when it comes to these narcotic substances, the Shari'ah does look at the uses and the causes. Generally speaking, with the mukhaddirat, you can look at the reason why it is used and pronounce a verdict based upon that, whereas with the muskirat, it doesn't matter what you use it for; the muskirat are all haram.

And the simplest example that all of us will understand is that before you do an operation, the anesthesiologist comes and he knocks you out. After the operation, you might have to take morphine. Morphine is a type of mukhaddir. Or when you're knocked out, you can categorize that as a type of mukhaddir. And it is permissible to be knocked out before you go into surgery. That's not muskirat; it is not an intoxication. It is something that has effects that at some level overlap, but there is also a difference between them.

And with this in mind, before we move on: so I talked about THC in the cannabis, and the THC is what causes the high or the elation. There is one more substance that you should be familiar with, and that is a cannabinoid, or the CBD. And the CBD is different than the THC. The CBD is that which causes the numbness or the lethargy; that's different. To feel numb and to feel calm, that generally comes with the CBD. The THC is what makes you euphoric, or your mind goes, you get stoned, you get high. That's what the THC does.

Now, both of these substances are present in the cannabis. However, how it is produced, how it is manufactured, how it is sold, you have different percentages and concentrations of THC and CBD. I hope that is clear. The final product — these days in America, almost half the states permit cannabis use for medicinal purposes, and very few states even have it for recreational purposes as well — the final product has many different varieties; it's not just one. And some of these products have higher percentages of CBD, and others have higher percentages of THC. And remember, it is the THC that causes you to be high, and it is the CBD that causes you to be more on the calm side.

Now, given that overall cannabis or marijuana does indeed cause that feeling of euphoria, along with the clouding of the senses, there is no question that when cannabis is used recreationally, i.e. to have fun, i.e. to get high, when you use cannabis just for the sake of entertainment, just for the sake of fun — there is no question, and I do not know of any reputable scholar that has another opinion — that this mukhaddir will take the ruling of the muskir. It will take the ruling of alcohol. And therefore, what intoxicates in large quantities will be haram in small quantities.

And that is why the position of all of the fuqaha that I'm familiar with is that marijuana in all of its forms is impermissible to use or to inhale or in any way ingest for the sake of pleasure and recreation. So marijuana, cannabis, anything that is derived from this, that is ingested for the purpose of pleasure, for the purpose of recreation, takes the ruling of the muskir, and it will be haram, and anybody who does so is sinful in the eyes of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

That having been said, as we said, the mukhaddirat and the muskirat are not always the same. And therefore, there are variations of cannabis in which the CBD component is found in higher concentrations than the THC. And generally speaking, it is those products that are said to be of benefit for a very, very specific, very narrow range of medicinal issues: for example, epilepsy; for example, to numb the side effects of radiotherapy.

So I'm assuming your relative, your cousin, or whoever it is, your sister — by the way, may Allah 'azza wa jall cure her or him and make it easy for them and for all of you. It's a very difficult situation, terminal cancer, and I can only make du'a. It's a very difficult situation, and may Allah make it all easy for the entire family.

So generally speaking, the cannabis that is prescribed for cancer patients or for epileptic patients is a type of cannabis in which the CBD component is the more pronounced one rather than the THC. And there is some discernible effect, as far as the modern literature says, for very specific issues like, as we said, epilepsy, or like the side effects of some types of radiotherapy, where the CBD does actually have a calming and a soothing effect, and it helps to cope with that pain or with the bouts of epilepsy.

And therefore, with respect to medicinal usages, a number of modern councils, including the Fiqh Council of North America, have said that in genuine cases of medicinal need — and every council that says this stresses: don't make it a game. Don't just say, oh, I have a headache and I have a need. Everybody knows that that's what's happening in the modern world: you just go and say, I have a migraine, I need my prescription for marijuana. That doesn't work that way. That's why most fiqh councils say, in order to allow for this concession — because it is going to be allowed in the end, as you have already figured out — you must have a reputable Muslim doctor.

Why a Muslim doctor? It's not that we don't trust a non-Muslim, but we expect the Muslim to understand the dangers of opening this door, because marijuana is a gateway drug. Everybody knows this; every study has shown this. Even if marijuana is not as bad as, let's say, crack cocaine, the Shari'ah is not based on whether it is as bad as or not when it comes to haram or halal. When something is haram — no doubt the sin might be worse if it is worse — but it is still haram. Just because beer is not as intoxicating as vodka or rum, it doesn't mean that beer is halal. It's still haram. Beer is haram and vodka is haram.

So a lot of our youth, they feel that our scholars are not aware of the fatwas of marijuana and whatnot, and they feel that, oh, it's no big deal. And the fact of the matter is that we are fully aware of this issue, and we understand that it's not as bad as other drugs out there, but it does not change the fact that it is a narcotic. And even if it is the least narcotic, it is still a narcotic. And it is a gateway, as study after study has shown: once you open this door, you want more and more. And so even from the avenue of closing the avenues — there's something called closing the doors to evil in the Shari'ah, sadd adh-dhari'ah — even from this avenue, we're going to shut this door. And also from the fact that there is no doubt that marijuana is a narcotic and a drug, we say that it is haram recreationally.

However, as we said, mukhaddir and muskir are not the same ruling, according to the more precise definition. There are some 'ulama, by the way, who just lumped them all together, and I can understand that, but it's not the same. And I'll give you some examples at the end that clearly demonstrate that it is not the same. The mukhaddir is not the same as the muskir. And I gave you the example of morphine as well, and others of this nature.

Now, as I said, the Fiqh Council and others have said that if there is a genuine medicinal need that has been testified to by a reputable Muslim doctor, who understands how evil this chapter is, then it is the lesser of the two evils. If a child is having epileptic fits, and taking a type of cannabis that has CBD in it calms the epilepsy; or there's somebody struggling with a great amount of pain because of the cancer radiation, and the cannabis helps them to cope with that, and helps them to cope with the side effects, of not vomiting and whatnot — in this case, it's the lesser of two evils. This is not recreational. And therefore, in that case, it will be allowed, because the mukhaddir is not a muskir.

You are never allowed to take a muskir for the sake of medicine. When a person came to our Prophet and said, I drink alcohol to help me with my disease, the Prophet said, it is not a cure; it is a disease. Alcohol — when I say alcohol, I mean of course alcoholic drinks — they are the disease. There is never a circumstance that you will take wine or beer for the sake of medicine. That's not going to work. It's not a medicine; it is the disease.

However, the mukhaddir is not the muskir, as we said, and the hadith of the muskirat, that the Prophet said it is not a cure, it is a disease, does not apply to the other category of substances called the mukhaddirat. And it is allowed to ingest that which is mukhaddir for the sake of averting a bigger disaster or a bigger calamity. And I gave the examples of epileptic fits, or of people that are having side effects because of radiation or whatever: if it is noticed and demonstrated — and of course the Muslim doctor will know the cases — then inshallah ta'ala it is permissible to do.

And by the way, just as a footnote here, this whole conversation about mukhaddir and muskir plays a broader role than just cannabis. The classic example here is nutmeg. One can even say vanilla extract in some sense, even though that's a slightly different case, but still, nutmeg is the classic example here. In our culture, in Indian-Pakistani culture, nutmeg is very, very common. We use it for many, many cuisines, and the average Pakistani, Indian, Bengali household has nutmeg in its cabinet.

And a lot of people don't know this, but in fact nutmeg is a type of mukhaddir, if it is used in large quantities. And it has been used by the native Indians; they would use it to get high on nutmeg. They have a way that they would do this, and they would become high. And every few years or so, you hear a case in the news of some lady or some man, they drink too much of their nutmeg — they have a drink, eggnog, that they put nutmeg in — and sometimes by accident, or sometimes on purpose, they become intoxicated by the nutmeg, or they have effects and they have to go to the hospital. So nutmeg is a mukhaddir.

Now, is nutmeg haram? If we were to say it is haram, a lot of our cooks and our aunties will be very angry: how dare you make this haram? And the response is that, well, firstly, some 'ulama did say that nutmeg is haram, because, as I said, some 'ulama did not differentiate between mukhaddir and muskir, and they said everything that is mukhaddir will take the ruling of muskir. And that is their position. However, the more discerning of the 'ulama, and the more research-based, and the ones who look in deeper and are not superficial or simplistic, they understand that mukhaddir is not the same as muskir.

And for this, again, I have many quotes here. So for example, the famous Shafi'i faqih al-Ramli, he was asked in his Fatawa, is it allowed to use nutmeg or not? (By the way, nutmeg is called jawz at-tib.) And he said, yes, it is allowed if it is used in small quantities; however, if it is used in large quantities, it will be haram. This is one of the greatest Shafi'i imams, al-Ramli. Also in the Hanafi book Radd al-Muhtar, again, they were asked about nutmeg, and he said that it is permissible to use small quantities of nutmeg and other substances; he has a list over here of what constitutes mukhaddir.

Why? Because in small quantities, as all of us know from our culture, a small quantity of nutmeg has no impact whatsoever. You don't get high or elation or euphoria; nothing happens. A large quantity will impact you. Now, if nutmeg had been a muskir, then it would be haram to take even a speck of it, because what did the Prophet ﷺ say? "Ma askara kathiruhu fa qaliluhu haram": whatever intoxicates in large will be haram in small. But nutmeg is not a muskir. And similarly, CBD is not a muskir; it is a mukhaddir.

So if there is a reason to do it that is greater — and this is something that, again, you weigh for every substance. So don't assume that nutmeg and CBD have the same ruling. They're in the same category, the same genus; they're both mukhaddirat. But then the scholar, the faqih, looks at the impact of CBD and looks at the impact of nutmeg. So yes, nutmeg and CBD are in the same category of mukhaddirat, but the ruling is not going to be exactly the same, because we know CBD does have an impact even at small quantities that nutmeg does not. Nutmeg at small quantities has no impact other than flavor. Absolutely no impact other than flavor. So there is not even karahah; you can use it without any prohibition, a small quantity for your food to change the taste. As for CBD, it does have an impact, and therefore it should not be done recreationally. We don't want to open this door whatsoever. If it is something that is genuinely done for the sake of battling a bigger issue or a bigger disease, then inshallah it is permissible.

And I want to read to you the fatwa from the Fiqh Council of North America. You will find it on its website, but I want to read it to you so that you are familiar with it. The Fiqh Council has a fatwa that was issued on December 2nd, 2018, on the use of marijuana:

"Question: What is the Islamic stance on using marijuana for recreational or medical purposes? Answer: The Fiqh Council recognizes that the cannabis plant, which is used to produce marijuana, contains high concentrations of two chemicals: tetrahydrocannabinol, THC, and cannabidiol, which is CBD. THC is psychoactive and causes consumers to alter their experience of reality, causing them to become high or intoxicated. CBD, on the other hand, does not cause such an effect. The prohibition of alcoholic beverages is well known in Islam. Muslim scholars throughout history have explained that wine was prohibited due to its intoxicating effects (iskar), and that any other substance which results in the same must have the same ruling. Furthermore, the Prophet ﷺ said, 'Every intoxicant is like wine, and every intoxicant is haram.' Therefore, any use of marijuana which can make a user intoxicated is forbidden in Islam."

This is the recreational side. Now, the fatwa goes on: "Some contemporary research argues that cannabis with varying concentrations of THC and CBD may be an effective treatment for certain diseases, such as relieving nausea for chemotherapy patients, or increasing appetite for HIV/AIDS patients, or reducing pain for neurological disorders and autoimmune diseases like arthritis. Some preparations of the cannabis plant contain a higher amount of CBD and a lower amount of THC. If these products do not intoxicate a user when consumed in large quantities, they are permissible to use in Islam for medical purposes only."

So this is very clear in this fatwa: if it does not intoxicate and it is needed. And this, as I said, is when the CBD is the one that is emphasized rather than the THC. The fatwa goes on: "There are some preparations of the cannabis plant with higher levels of THC that are claimed to be more effective for certain illnesses when used as medicine." Now we're entering a gray area here. "Many scholars of the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools of Islamic law accept that it is permissible to use unlawful substances, such as pig byproducts, for medicinal purposes when there is no alternative available and it is known that the cure lies in the medication. The Fiqh Council adopts a similar position, but cautions that these conditions must strictly be observed, since it is common for people to claim flimsy excuses, such as minor aches and pains, as an excuse to use marijuana in order to get intoxicated."

Now, before I move on: the Fiqh Council demarcates two categories of substances. The first of them is that the product that is being used has the emphasis on the CBD: there's a high amount of CBD and a lower amount of THC. And generally speaking, such substances do not intoxicate even when used in larger quantities. And in that circumstance, there is really no problem to use these products for medicinal purposes.

And by the way, there are certain creams and lotions and whatnot that have CBD and hardly any THC, and if you were to apply the whole bottle on you, it will not impact you in any manner. That is of course permitted, because there is no THC, or the THC is so negligible that it has no impact on you. The fatwa is not talking about that, because that doesn't even apply. What the fatwa is saying is that there is an amount of THC, but it's not enough to really bring about the intoxication, and the main purpose would be to have an effective treatment for certain diseases. In this case, they said it is permissible for medicinal use.

Now, they then entered a gray area. What if the THC is indeed higher? What if there is an amount of intoxication? And the fatwa simply says it's a gray area; really, it's a case-by-case basis. Look at the sickness and how bad it is, and is it really worth getting this substance involved? And if there is no alternative, then some 'ulama have allowed the use of haram. By haram, we mean here non-alcoholic haram, because there's, as we said, mukhaddir, and there's, as we said, muskirat, and there's other things as well. So again, pig products, for example.

I mean, again, the issue comes — for example, there was a case that I had to deal with. The heart of a young girl — there was some issue, and there was some tissue that needed to be put in the heart. And the doctor said that, for whatever reason, the only tissue that would work is that which is coming from a pig. And obviously the fatwa here is: completely permissible. She's not going to live if she doesn't get that tissue replacement. And so you use that pig part, because it is darurah; it is something that is a necessity. And in that type of life situation, then of course it is completely permitted.

So the point being that when the pain or when the suffering is so bad, and a substance is calming or helping at a certain level — the substance is not going to be muskir, it's going to be mukhaddir — in this case, the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools, many of them, allowed the use of that which is haram for medicinal purposes, if it is proven that there is no alternative and there is cure in that.

And the final point of the Fiqh Council is that "the Fiqh Council warns Muslims from investing in the marijuana industry, since the overwhelming majority of this business is for recreational purposes. The Council also encourages that more research be done on the medical benefits of marijuana to determine whether there are any other substitutes for the psychoactive preparations of the product in treating illnesses." End quote.

In other words, sorry, you can't invest in marijuana stocks. You're not going to get rich off of that, and even if you do, there's going to be no barakah. Do not invest in marijuana stocks. And the Fiqh Council is saying that Muslim doctors need to verify, because we don't know: is this being hyped up, the use of medicinal marijuana? Is there an alternative or not? We don't know. So we encourage doctors, we encourage scientists, to do research to find out: is there an alternative, so that we don't have to worry whether there's a mukhaddir or not? And whether this is an actual, genuine medicine in these circumstances. Because still — I mean, again, I'm not a medical expert, but I've spoken to a number of doctors in the field — doctors themselves disagree amongst themselves: is this something effective or not?

So it's not the job of 'ulama to give specific prescriptions. The 'ulama speak in generalities, and the doctors then take those generalities. The general rule has been explained to you, and that is that the mukhaddir and the muskir are not the same, and the mukhaddir can be used if there is an overwhelming need, a medicinal need. And that is why morphine is allowed when you're in extreme pain, even though there are effects of morphine that are, generally speaking, not allowed. You would not be allowed to take morphine for recreational use, but it is allowed when you need to numb the pain.

When you go into an operation, you need to basically be knocked out. That is completely allowed. Otherwise, you're not supposed to do that for recreational purposes. You're not supposed to take anything that will intentionally knock you out. You don't do that. But now there's a greater good, and that greater good is the surgery, the procedure that needs to be done. It cannot be done when you are awake.

So understand this point: mukhaddir and muskir. And generally speaking, mukhaddirat take the ruling of muskirat when they are used for pleasure. Is that clear? That should be very clear now. The mukhaddirat and the muskirat take the same ruling — I need to point out here — they take the same ruling, that it is haram. But some of our fuqaha have said that the hadd punishment will be less for the mukhaddir than it will be for the muskir. And some have said... so again, there's a bit of a controversy about this; it's separate. But they will take the same ruling when it comes to a sin. However, if the mukhaddir is used for medicinal purposes, then the ruling changes, and we have a little bit more leeway, as we said, in this regard.

Now, the final question that our brother had here is about the cancer patient: if he or she has to take it, and then they are knocked out, they're otherwise incapacitated, they cannot pray. He is asking, is the prayer forgiven, or should we have the person make up the prayer afterwards?

So to answer this question, we can state that, generally speaking, when a person is sick, especially in this type of extreme pain, high fever, or terminal cancer with radiotherapy going on, then it is completely permissible, 100% halal, to combine Dhuhr and Asr, and Maghrib and Isha, as if you were traveling. So just like when you're traveling, you pray Dhuhr and Asr together at one time, and then Maghrib and Isha at one time, so too when you're in extreme illness or pain, radiotherapy, all of this stuff, it is permissible that you do so.

If you're able to take this substance, this medicinal cannabis, such that you've prayed your Dhuhr and Asr and then you take this for pain relief, and then by the time you wake up, your Maghrib and Isha will come without any haraj, then inshallah that is ideal. And again, Dhuhr and Asr, you take it as one timeframe. Maghrib and Isha, from the beginning of Maghrib all the way till Fajr, that is one timeframe. And if you're able to do that, perfect.

However, if you're not able to, and the pain is too severe and you are forced to take it, and the amount basically knocks you out, in this case, **you are forgiven from the wujub of praying, but you are not forgiven from the wujub of qada.** And this goes back to the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: "Man nama 'an salatin aw nasiyaha fal-yusalliha idha dhakaraha, la kaffarata laha illa dhalik": whoever amongst you forgets to pray or accidentally oversleeps the prayer, then let him pray when he remembers; there is no kaffarah other than that. There is no expiation; you don't have to do anything more other than to make up the prayer that you missed.

Now in this case, we can give him the same ruling, even though he didn't forget; he intentionally went to sleep, but he was excused. He needed to put himself to sleep, or he needed to take the medication for the pain. So in this case, we say: dear brother or sister, if you must take this medication to battle your pain and it knocks you out, if you are not able to schedule it such that your Dhuhr and Asr and then Maghrib and Isha are prayed in their proper time, then you may take it.

> لا يكلف الله نفسا إلا وسعها
>
> وما جعل عليكم في الدين من حرج
>
> ولن يشاد هذا الدين أحد إلا غلبه

So many ahadith about not making Islam difficult. Those who make Islam too strict and whatnot have destroyed themselves. Allah wants to make things easy.

> لا ضرر ولا ضرار

The Shari'ah has come for yusr, for samahah. There are so many principles of fiqh that state we do not make the religion more difficult. This is a person suffering from terminal cancer; they're having serious pain. SubhanAllah, you're going to tell this person, don't take the medication? On the contrary. If they're able to, as we said, schedule, go ahead. If not, take the medication. If you're knocked out, when you wake up, then you make up the salawat that you missed when you were knocked out.

And subhanAllah, if you're not able to pray standing, then pray sitting; if not, then lying down. This is a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: "Salli qa'iman, fa in lam tastati' fa qa'idan, fa in lam tastati' fa 'ala janb": pray standing up; if you cannot, then pray sitting down; if you cannot, then on your side. Whatever situation you can do. And if you cannot even go to the bathroom, then do wudu with a little bit of water in front of you. If water cannot touch your skin, do tayammum. SubhanAllah, don't make Islam more difficult. Allah wants to make things easy, and the Shari'ah has given you all of these concessions.

So the bottom line, to summarize and conclude — a long fatwa, but it was necessary: **there is no question that marijuana in all of its forms is haram when it is used for recreation.** And I remind all of my brothers and sisters, especially the young brothers and sisters, to fear Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and do not take this as a joke. This is not a joke. This is not a joke. You're opening up the door of Shaytan. When you think that it is a trivial matter, you're opening up the door of Shaytan. You're causing issues with your prayer, with your concentration, with spending money; you're causing issues with having companions that are evil. Everything about the industry is evil, and the whole entertainment, the whole issue of this drug, it is a stepping stone, a gateway to far worse than this. And it is something that is definitely sinful in the eyes of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Repent to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and get rid of this.

As for those that have genuine medical issues, and reputable Muslim doctors have said to them that certain compounds that have CBD would help them, inshallah, for them it is not the same as the recreational use. And if there is a need, then indeed — and Allah knows, and they have to answer in front of Allah. You don't come to me; you know whether you need it or not, and your doctor will consult with you. If there is a genuine need, then inshallah, it is permitted for the greater good. And Allah knows best.
